Roofing in Kingwood, TX

Kingwood has been part of the City of Houston since 1996, so a new roof needs a Houston permit, and the tall pines decide how fast it wears. Call one free number at any hour to reach an independent, locally owned roofing company.

Kingwood is a Houston neighborhood with its own feel

Roofing in Kingwood, TX runs on City of Houston rules. People who moved to the Livable Forest for its trees and its villages sometimes forget that, and it matters the day a roof needs replacing.

Kingwood was laid out as a master-planned community in the far northeast corner of Harris County, where the San Jacinto's West Fork widens into Lake Houston, and a small part of it crosses into Montgomery County. The city's own area profile notes three things a roofer would also notice: the woods are thick, the houses vary a great deal in size and style, and Humble ISD, not Houston ISD, serves most of the area.

It is not a separate city. Houston annexed the commercial entrance in 1995 and the residential areas on December 11, 1996. Since then, re-roof permits, inspections and code questions for Kingwood homes go to the Houston Permitting Center, the same office that handles a house in the Heights or Meyerland.

Houston Expert Roofers does none of the roofing. It is a no-cost number: the automated assistant takes the call at any hour, hears what the roof is doing and which village you are in, and connects you with an independent, locally owned roofing company. Inspection, the written estimate, the permit and the work all belong to that company, and it bills you directly.

City of Houston roofing permit rules, as they apply in Kingwood

These come from the Houston Permitting Center's residential roofing permit page and the city's storm notices. A roofer that works Kingwood regularly should know them without looking them up.

  • Small repairsRoof covering work up to 100 square feet in total is exempt from a permit.
  • Re-roof or overlayNeeds a City of Houston residential roofing permit, pulled before work starts.
  • Structural changesAltering rafters, trusses or the roof's shape needs plans, not only a roofing permit.
  • Deed restrictionsAfter the May 2024 derecho the city reminded owners that repairs must also follow their deed restrictions.

After the 2024 derecho the city expedited re-roof and overlay permits so owners could get storm repairs moving, but it did not drop the requirement. If a roofer offers to skip the permit to save a few days, the inspection and the record of the work go with it, and an unpermitted re-roof can come up when you sell. Ask to see the permit before tear-off.

Many Kingwood sections also have a community association with its own architectural review. Where yours does, get written approval for the shingle style and color before the city permit is filed, so neither one holds up the other.

What a forest does to a roof

The trees are the reason most people choose Kingwood, and they are also the main reason Kingwood roofs wear the way they do. A roofer quoting here should look up before it looks at the shingles.

Needles in the valleys

Pine straw slides down the roof and packs into valleys, behind chimneys and against the uphill side of skylights. It holds water against the underlayment and the flashing long after the rain stops. Leaks that only show up after a long, soaking rain often start there. The flashing repair page shows where those joints are.

Slopes that never fully dry

North-facing slopes under a full canopy can stay damp for days, which feeds algae streaks and moss and, over years, can soften the decking underneath. Algae-resistant shingles, which carry copper or zinc granules, slow the streaking on a new roof.

Limbs and whole trees

Tall pines with a big crown catch wind. In a strong storm a limb can crack shingles or punch through the deck, and a whole tree on a house is a structural job, not a roofing patch. Stay out from under it and keep away from any line it brought down.

Stay off the roof. Wet, storm-damaged roofs are slick and the decking may be weak, so leave the ladder in the garage. Keep well away from downed power lines and report them to CenterPoint Energy or 911. Indoors, move belongings away from the leak, put a bucket or towels under the drip and keep people out of any room where the ceiling sags. Photograph the damage from the ground and inside the house, then call your insurer and a roofer.

Kingwood's storm record, from annexation to Beryl

Not every Kingwood storm was a roof storm. The floods did their damage from the ground up, while wind and falling trees work from the top down. A roofer looking at a Kingwood house should know which of these the home has been through.

WhenWhat happenedRoof angle
December 1996The City of Houston annexed Kingwood's residential areas on December 11.City of Houston permits apply to every re-roof since.
August 2017Harvey. The West Fork gauge at US 59 in Humble passed 62 feet and was still rising, per Community Impact. Local estimates cited in City of Houston dredging updates put the damage around the lake at upward of 16,000 homes.Flood damage, not roof damage, for most homes. Rebuilt houses may have had attic work skipped.
May and September 2019The Harris County Flood Control District says the Kingwood area flooded twice more, the second time in Tropical Storm Imelda.Mostly drainage flooding. Wind-driven rain also tested older flashing.
May 16, 2024A derecho with winds over 100 mph in parts of the metro, per the National Weather Service. Houston expedited re-roof permits afterward.Lifted shingles and limbs on roofs across the city.
July 8, 2024Hurricane Beryl knocked out power to more than two million CenterPoint Energy customers.Trees and limbs on houses across greater Houston.

Flood and wind are covered by different policies. Water rising from the river or a gully is a flood claim under a separate flood policy, while a limb through the roof or wind-lifted shingles fall under a homeowners policy. Ask your insurer which applies before anyone starts work, and read the roof insurance claims guide.

Why Kingwood homeowners call the line

A roof that has reached its age

Much of Kingwood was built in waves, so whole sections reach replacement age together. Owners call to have a roofer tell them, with photos, whether theirs has years left or is shedding granules and curling at the edges.

A limb through the roof

After a strong storm the call is urgent: water in the house and a hole overhead. The roofing company decides how to dry it in safely. You stay off the roof and away from the tree.

A permit and an approval to line up

Between the city permit and an association's review, a Kingwood re-roof has more paperwork than one in unincorporated Harris County. Callers want a company that has done it before and knows the order.

A leak that only shows in long rains

Drips that appear only after a day of steady rain usually trace back to a needle-packed valley, a skylight curb or a chimney. Finding them takes an attic inspection as well as a look at the shingles.

Questions for a roofer working in Kingwood

Permits and approvals

  • Will you pull the City of Houston residential roofing permit in your company's name?
  • Does my section's association need to approve the shingle color, and who submits it?
  • Will you show me the permit before tear-off and the final inspection when you finish?

The roof itself

  • Which valleys and flashings are holding needles and water, and how will the new roof handle them?
  • Do you recommend algae-resistant shingles under this canopy?
  • What is your per-sheet price for decking, and your workmanship warranty in writing?
  • Can you send a certificate of liability insurance made out to me?

How a Kingwood call works

  1. Call the numberAn automated assistant answers (832) 662-4107 at any hour and asks which service you need, since the line also takes heating, cooling, pressure washing and water damage calls.
  2. Describe the roofA leak, missing shingles, hail, a limb on the roof or an old roof you want looked at, plus your part of greater Houston and how urgent it is.
  3. Get put throughYour call is transferred to an independent, locally owned roofing company, which hears a short summary before it picks up.
  4. Deal with the roofer directlyIt inspects, quotes and does the work, and you pay it (or your insurer does, as you arrange). If it misses the call, it gets your name, number, city and need to call you back.

Texas has no state roofing license. No state agency licenses roofing contractors in Texas, and a 2025 bill to create one (HB 3344) did not reach a vote of the full House before the session ended. So check what you can: a certificate of liability insurance sent to you, a written contract with the full scope, a permit where your city requires one, local addresses you can drive past, and the shingle maker's warranty registration. Some cities also ask roofers to register. The line does not check any of this for you. How to check a roofer before you hire.

The deductible is yours to pay. The Texas Department of Insurance says it is illegal for a contractor to offer to waive, rebate or absorb your deductible, and a contract of $1,000 or more paid with insurance money must include a notice saying so. A roofer also may not act as your public adjuster on a property it works on. Treat any offer to "cover the deductible" as a reason to call someone else.

Questions Houston homeowners ask

Does a Kingwood re-roof need a city permit?

Yes. Kingwood is inside the City of Houston, and the Houston Permitting Center requires a residential roofing permit for a re-roof or an overlay. Roof covering work that does not exceed 100 square feet in total is exempt, so a small repair usually needs no permit. Changing the framing that holds the roof up is a bigger job that needs plans. Ask the roofer to pull the permit in its own name. Details are in the permit section.

When did Houston annex Kingwood?

City of Houston records put it in two steps: the shopping strip at the entrance in 1995, then the neighborhoods themselves on December 11, 1996. Several of Kingwood's municipal utility districts were absorbed in that annexation, and a tax increment zone for the Lake Houston area, TIRZ 10, was set up to replace them. That is why City of Houston rules apply to every Kingwood roof.

Can I just call 311 about a roof problem in Kingwood?

311 is the City of Houston's line for city services, such as a tree blocking a street or a general permit question. It does not send a roofer. For a leak or storm damage, call the free line to be put through to an independent roofing company, and call CenterPoint Energy or 911 about any downed power line. The emergency roof repair page lists safe first steps.

Why do Kingwood roofs get dark streaks and moss?

Shade and moisture. City planners call Kingwood's setting heavily wooded, and slopes under a thick canopy dry slowly after rain, which lets algae and moss grow. Algae streaks are mostly cosmetic, but moss holds water against the shingles. Ask a roofer about algae-resistant shingles on a replacement, and see the roof inspection page for what a full check covers.

Who comes out when I call about roofing in Kingwood, TX?

An independent, locally owned roofing company that takes Kingwood calls. Houston Expert Roofers is only the phone line: its automated assistant picks up around the clock, notes the problem and your neighborhood, and passes the call on. Inspection, quoting, the city permit and the work itself are the roofing company's to handle, and the roofer, not the line, is who you pay. Calling is free, and companies may pay the line a referral fee.
